title: How the IV-fluid supply works in this scenario
statement: The structure of the scenario is a deterministic assumption, chosen for this scenario. 100 hospitals each have a part of their demand that is critical in a shortage: resuscitation and other essential care. Each hospital uses its own reserve. While the affected maker cannot ship, the supply from unaffected manufacturers goes to resuscitation. When released fluid arrives, it meets both demands, and the unaffected supply goes to hospitals outside the study area. Each patient gets one complete course of resuscitation. RT-SECTOR-SC10-2026 chooses the operating values, and A-SC10-CONSEQUENCES-2026 chooses the clinical and economic values.
rationale: Stocks follow the typical 15 to 22 days on hand reported before the 2024 shortage. The unaffected share follows the market share of the affected maker, roughly 60%. With these values, resuscitation stock lasts until release starts again in two cases. In the first, the attacker is cut off. In the second, the manufacturer resets its record credentials before the attacker acts. So at the defaults, harm to resuscitation patients is zero on those pathways. The shortage then falls on other essential care, counted as lost value and days without fluid. Resuscitation patients are harmed where a hold on released lots empties their reserve, or where stock is smaller. No study of fluid shortages estimates the clinical values. Two kinds of evidence bracket them. Septic-shock mortality rose 3.7 points during a vasopressor shortage. Studies of saline shortages found no mortality signal.

supports.note: Typical supply was 15 to 22 days on hand before the shortage.
Most hospitals that responded held a stock of large-volume fluid for two weeks to a month at baseline.
Before the shortage, no hospital that responded held less than three days of IV fluid.
The affected plant made about 60% of US IV solutions, so others supplied about 40%.
Hospitals protected fluid for shock resuscitation and used less for other care.
Septic-shock mortality rose 3.7 points during a norepinephrine shortage. This gives an upper limit for context; it is not an estimate for fluid.
A saline-shortage cohort showed no mortality difference.
A trial in which all patients get active treatment cannot show the harm of no fluid.

One blood supplier hit by ransomware serves more than 250 hospitals, and it asked all of them to activate critical shortage protocols (31 Jul 2024 capture, paras 1-5). The request to hospitals is in the 31 Jul capture, at most 2.7 d after the start on 29 Jul.
NYBCe serves more than 400 hospitals and collects about 4,000 units/day (The Record, 30 Jan 2025, paras 1-2)
1,032 ED patients with severe sepsis or septic shock at one tertiary centre, Jan 2014-May 2017. 1,032 / 1,247 d = 0.83 per day (abstract).
For low-acuity ED visits, saline use fell from 5.5% to 2.0% (nausea/vomiting) and from 6.6% to 2.5% (dehydration). These are relative falls of about 64% and 62% (Results).
60% reserved or restricted fluids for certain indications. 17% cancelled or delayed voluntary procedures. 84% reported a moderate or critical impact (Key Findings).

More than 81% ran protocols to save fluid, and nearly 17% cancelled elective procedures (body paras 1-2, 4-6). More than 81% had these protocols by 7-8 Oct 2024 (body paras). Gray-market sellers offered fluid at marked-up prices to more than 40% of respondents. This is a cost to hospitals, but the source does not quantify it.
Perioperative IV-fluid restriction in 2,028 matched patients showed no difference in mortality or morbidity (abstract). Perioperative restriction: no difference in mortality (abstract).
Downstream losses occurred only at customers with 1-4 alternative suppliers. Customers with 5 or more had no loss (Table 4 col. 3).

From 9 Oct 2024, allocation rose from 40% to 60% for direct customers and from 10% to 60% for distributors. Children's hospitals got 100%, and 90-100% was expected by year end (paras 1-2). HHS and FDA committed to faster imports and to shelf-life extensions (AHA 9 Oct 2024, para 4).
Product allocations of 40-80% rose to 100% on 17 Dec or 31 Dec 2024 (D5NS expected mid-Jan). Allocations were based on the orders of each facility in Mar-Aug 2024 (PDF pp.1-2 tables).

Temporary import of 40 IV/PD products from seven plants of the same manufacturer (31 Oct 2024 bulletin). Limits: this route may close if the maker's own systems for orders, quality release or distribution are impaired. Import facilitation reported 31 Oct 2024.
10 of 16 studies of drug shortages reported higher mortality. The review gives no pooled effect (Results).
170 patients were harmed (mostly 'low harm'), and the attack contributed to 1 death (The Register 26 Jun 2025, paras 1-6). The source gives no denominator.
By week 15, 10,146 outpatient appointments and 1,705 elective procedures were postponed (NHS England London, 19 Sep 2024).
Fully operational at most 16 d after detection on 4 May (8-K/A 20 May 2026). No unauthorized activity after 5 May, day 1.
This source disagrees: in many cases, notPetya victims stopped work for about 3-4 weeks (Sec. 5.1).
This source disagrees: all facilities were fully operational 4 d after the attack (3 Jun 2021 release).
UK production stopped for about 5 weeks. CMC models a straight-line recovery to full output by early Jan 2026 (an assumption of the CMC model).
Automated order processing started again 42 d after the announcement on 14 Aug. The company restocks 'over time' (4 Oct 2023 release).
Orders through the system started again on day 64-65, and logistics were normal by Feb 2026 (recurrence release).
Restoration of shipping began on day 9, but the work through the backlog 'will take time' (3 Sep 2026 update).
The company disconnected its network and isolated its data centre about 4 h after the disruption.
At day 9, the company believed the issue was 'materially contained'.
By 18 Sep, day 35, the company wrote that it 'believes' the activity is 'contained'.
Q1 FY24 net sales were $1,386M against $1,740M (USD2023). Attack costs were about $24M in Q1, and $40-50M are expected for FY24 (USD2023, 25.4 and 42.3-52.8 USD2025m).
About $400M of sales lost in FY2025 (USD2025). About $26M of extra costs in Q4 (USD2025).

Net sales over 6 months were $79M below the prior year, after a shortfall of $354M in Q1. So (354-79)/354 = 78% was recovered, and about 22% was not recovered by 6 months. Price, mix and FX confound this (Q2 FY24 release).
In the quarter with an incident of at most 16 d, sales rose 13.8% and guidance was raised. So the permanent loss is about 0.
'expect to lose some further revenue permanently' (RNS 6 Jul 2017)
'anticipates recovering some portion of the impacted revenue'
A remaining effect of about $0.15/share in Q1 2024. The company expects to recover merchandise sales.
Affected customers added 13-15% more alternative suppliers within 6 months and ended ties with the hit supplier after more than 1 year.
One-time professional fees $11M (USD2023, 11.62 USD2025m)
Investigation, recovery and remediation $20M within $60M, of which $40M was demurrage (USD2022, 22.0 USD2025m)
$593M direct response costs, including medical-care costs (USD2024; outlier)
The profit loss of customers was about 4x the damages that the hit firms reported ($7.3B against $1.8B; the quantities are not alike).
In its 4 August 2024 statement, OneBlood says the critical software systems it uses to manage daily operations have started to come back online.
In its report of May 11, 2026, seven days after it first detected the intrusion, West states that it had restored its core enterprise systems.
An ASPE data brief prepared by Eastern Research Group analyses national drug-product shortages that began between 2018 and 2023.

In a statement released 8 August 2025, the FDA Commissioner announced that the nationwide shortage of sodium chloride 0.9% injection products had officially ended. These products would be removed from the Current Shortages list of FDA's Drug Shortage Database.
A reason was given for about two-thirds of product shortages (1,337), and 523 of those (39.1%) said 'other'.
In an 8-K under Item 1.05 (date of report 7 September 2026), Boston Scientific states that on 25 August 2026 it identified a cybersecurity incident.

Clorox states that on 14 August 2023 it announced that it had identified unauthorized activity on some of its IT systems. It took steps to stop and remediate the activity, 'including taking certain systems offline'.

Cencora, Inc. reports in a Form 8-K signed February 27, 2024 that on February 21, 2024 it learned that data had been exfiltrated from its information systems. Some of the data possibly contained personal information.
Dr. Reddy's second-quarter FY21 results release, issued October 28, 2020, has a 'Cyber Attack Update' section.
Expeditors' public downtime log records the first week of its 2022 cyber-attack.

Sun Pharma's audited FY2022-23 consolidated statements cover the year to 31 March 2023. In them, Sun Pharma says that on 1 March 2023 the parent company disclosed an information security incident that affected some of the Group's IT assets.
West Pharmaceutical Services states in its May 11, 2026 Form 8-K that on May 7, 2026 it determined it had experienced a material cybersecurity attack.
A food processor's systems came back online within days of a 2021 ransomware attack.
Most of that processor's facilities were operational when it paid the ransom.
A 2025 carmaker shutdown was modelled at GBP 1.9 bn of UK impact, mostly from lost production.
The shutdown suggests at least a significant risk that attackers had reached operational technology.
A brewer restarted production at all six domestic factories within days of a 2025 ransomware attack, with shipments following.
Its October-December revenue ran at about 70-90% of the prior year across businesses.
A 2023 attack cut a consumer-goods maker's quarterly net sales by an expected 23-28%.
A logistics firm's enterprise systems came back in stages over weeks after a 2022 attack.
An injectable-components maker shut down and isolated affected infrastructure on detection in 2026.
After the 2024 hurricane the IV-fluid maker expected to restart its highest-throughput line within weeks.
Small-volume IV bags to two hospitals' operating rooms fell to zero after Hurricane Maria and stayed low for months.

evidence_needed: Stocks for the specific population, clinical demand, outcomes with clinical definitions and their denominators, the logistics of replacement supply, costs, and an independent clinical review.

title: How the attacker's actions and the response interact
statement: The model treats each of these as separate: access that the attacker set up in advance, operational demand, information integrity and independently verified recovery. The inputs of each defender response are the same in every attack it is paired with.
rationale: Removal of the attacker's foothold happens at the same time as restoration. At the default work rates, it is not the step that limits the time. RT-SC10-INTEGRITY-REVERIFY covers the extra work to verify records again, and A-SC10-RETAMPER covers the second attack. Hospital stock changes only through use, deliveries and holds on lots released on altered records. Independent supply is not affected.
evidence_needed: An independent operational review is needed. It should cover what the attacker observes, its access, detection at the first attempted use, recovery resources and timing. It should also cover how the impairment applies across the defender responses. The claims that support this assumption show only the type of mechanism. None of them states the hours, the area or the delivered capacity chosen for this scenario.

decided.by: Selected implementation-plan assumption; not independently scientifically reviewed

supports.note: Records must be kept with their metadata, and the relevant audit trails must be reviewed before batch release. That is why altered shipment records add work before qualified release.
Restoration of data is different from validation that the data matches its trusted version from before the corruption. Containment does not clear the list of records that still need reconciliation.
Before normal operation starts again, recovery checks the restored assets and deals with any compromise that continues.

title: IT ransomware at a dominant fluid maker stops deliveries to the hospitals
statement: Ransomware encrypts the release, labeling and shipment systems of a dominant maker of sterile fluid. From t=0 this stops its deliveries to the modeled hospitals for about 10.5, 21 or 35 days in the early, standard and limited responses. Each response sets its own duration. After that, product reaches the hospitals a day later through the distribution network. In the meantime, the hospitals use up their stock.
rationale: Documented halts at manufacturers and distributors start in IT systems. They stop order processing, release and shipment even where production equipment is intact. No documented cyber incident has caused an IV-fluid shortage. So the step from a halted release to empty hospital reserves is a stated premise, not a result taken from a source.
evidence_needed: A shortage record from a regulator that attributes a sterile-injectable or IV-fluid shortage to a cyber incident. Or data from suppliers and hospitals on how long release and shipment stopped after ransomware at a manufacturer, and whether allocation protected hospital reserves.

supports.note: A 2017 cyberattack disrupted the worldwide production of a pharmaceutical manufacturer. It could not fulfil orders for certain products in certain markets. The same report states that it continued to fulfil orders and ship product, and it names no product line that stopped.

A 2019 cyberattack cost an aluminium producer its production and its ability to process orders for a period in March and April. Its other business areas kept normal production only through work-intensive workarounds and manual procedures.
Ransomware that encrypted an operator's IT systems led it to halt all pipeline operations as a precaution; lines returned to operation within days.
Records must be kept with their metadata, and audit trails must be reviewed before batch release. So when release records are not available, release stops even if production can run.
A hurricane, not a cyberattack, disrupted production at a dominant IV-fluid maker. The result was a shortage, and FDA met it with requalification, testing before distribution and temporary imports.

This source disagrees: the regulator's register of biologics shortages attributes no listed shortage of that manufacturer to the attack. The one pediatric entry open in that period began before the attack.
After a ransomware attack, a blood supplier returned to normal distribution about 10 days after the start.
A device maker restored production, order fulfilment and shipping about 15 days after its incident.
A wholesaler restored electronic orders and returned operations to normal about 16 days after detection.
A freight forwarder had limited ability to operate for about three weeks.
Product takes a typical one to two weeks to flow through the distribution network after allocation changes.
About ten days after its incident, a distributor took and fulfilled orders again through manual channels.
Fully operational again in at most 16 d.
This source disagrees: 3-4 weeks in many cases.
A device maker disclosed in 2026 that an intrusion impaired production and the processing and shipping of orders.
Ransomware at a blood supplier in 2024 sent more than 250 hospitals to critical shortage protocols within about three days.
A 2024 cyber-attack on a pathology provider helped drive O-type blood stocks in England to unprecedentedly low levels; hospitals were told to restrict use.
The alert about blood stocks that the attack triggered ended after almost a year.
Ransomware hampered some production at an infusion-therapy maker in 2020.
This source disagrees: the same company said that the attack limited some operations, while patient care continued.
The ransomware family seeks processes tied to industrial control and manufacturing networks.
This source disagrees: a drugmaker said that its 2023 ransomware incident did not affect core systems and operations.
The same drugmaker later said network isolation impacted business operations and would reduce revenue in some businesses.
Its auditor made the incident a key audit matter and tested alternate controls during the breach.
This source disagrees: a drugmaker isolated its data centres after a 2020 attack and expected services back within 24 hours without major operational impact.
A 2023 incident primarily affected a healthcare distributor's North American and European distribution businesses.
The distributor's ecommerce platform was disrupted again 39 days after the first incident.
Ransomware affected every operating division of a blood-centre network in January 2025; systems were taken offline.
This source disagrees: blood centres nationwide supplied thousands of units within days, so mutual aid can cover a halted supplier.
A plasma collector took systems offline after an April 2024 attack. Eight days later, it announced that its 176 US donation centres had reopened.
The same attack forced the collector to shut operations for nearly a week.
In 2024, an actor associated with a nation state got into a healthcare payment network. The company isolated the affected systems and could not estimate the duration.
This source disagrees: the company said that it arranged workarounds so that patients could get their medicines during the outage.
Pharmacy services were largely restored about two weeks after onset.
Pharmacy claims were near normal about two months after onset.

elicitation.question: Does IT ransomware at a concentrated sterile-fluid manufacturer stop its deliveries to hospitals at once, and for long enough to draw down their reserved inventory?
elicitation.argument: Documented halts at manufacturers and distributors started in IT systems, through ransomware or wipers and precautionary shutdowns, not in the production process, and losing release, labeling and order systems stops shipment even with intact lines: a 2017 attack disrupted a pharmaceutical maker's worldwide manufacturing and order fulfilment, and a 2019 attack cost a manufacturer production and order processing over part of March and April. Recent disclosures report the same pattern: a medical-device maker stated in 2026 that an intrusion stopped manufacturing, order processing and shipping (E-BSX26-8K-OPS), and a 2024 ransomware attack on a US blood supplier sent more than 250 hospitals to shortage protocols (E-ONEBLOOD24-SHORTAGE). A 2024 attack on a London pathology provider led to a national alert on O-type blood stocks in England that lasted almost a year (E-NHSBT24-AMBER, E-NHSBT25-STANDDOWN), and in 2020 ransomware hampered some production at an infusion-therapy maker (E-CYBERSCOOP20-FRESENIUS-PRODUCTION). A 2024 hurricane at one plant producing about 60 percent of US IV solutions shows that interrupting one concentrated maker produces a national shortage.
elicitation.dissent: No cyber incident has caused an FDA-listed IV-fluid or sterile-injectable shortage, and the federal shortage-cause categories contain no cyber reason; the one pharmaceutical precedent continued to fulfil orders and ship product, and the regulator's register attributes none of its shortages to the attack. Large healthcare supply-chain intrusions have passed without supply effect: a major drug distributor breached in 2024 reported no material impact on its operations. Documented cyber halts at manufacturers lasted from days to several weeks, and in the 2024 physical shortage hospitals protected resuscitation and pediatric use by allocation and triage, so a cyber halt may never reach resuscitation reserves. In the analogs output rarely reached zero: suppliers kept shipping through manual workarounds, and allocation protected the most critical uses. Other pharmaceutical intrusions left core operations running or limited them briefly (E-SUNPHARMA23-INITIAL, E-DRL20-ISOLATE, E-KREBS20-FRESENIUS-LIMITED), and blood centres covered a halted peer within days by mutual aid (E-NYBCE25-MUTUALAID).
elicitation.falsifier: A regulator's shortage record attributing a sterile-injectable or IV-fluid shortage to a cyber incident would confirm the step; supplier or hospital data showing that allocation and triage kept resuscitation use supplied through a comparable halt would refute it.

title: If the attacker keeps write access, rechecks add 168 work-hours before qualified release
statement: When the attacker alters release and shipment records, the manufacturer must re-verify the affected batch and shipment records against a last-known-good version before qualified release. This adds 168 work-hours after its ordinary restoration work. Removal of the attacker stops further changes, but it does not do that work.
rationale: Data-integrity guidance requires records and audit trails to support release. Recovery that focuses on integrity treats the restoration of data and its validation as separate steps. Similar re-verification steps happened inside the restoration periods of other incidents: a blood supplier's manual labeling and record re-entry, and a device maker's product-quality analyses. So they limit the scale, but the model does not add them again here.
evidence_needed: A documented case in which an attacker altered pharmaceutical release or shipment records, and the time taken to re-verify them.

supports.note: Release depends on complete records with their audit trails.
Recovery restores data and checks that it matches its trusted version from before the corruption. These are separate steps.
After normal operations resumed, staff entered the donor records from the days of manual work again.
Analyses of product quality ended inside the restoration period.
The technique entry documents no stored-data manipulation of manufacturing or release records.
The attacker had access about 10 d before the disruption. Backups were suspended to protect integrity, and restore from backups was confirmed safe.
This source disagrees: systems 'cleared reverification' by day 6, inside the basic halt period.
This source disagrees: the only public manipulation altered leaked copies, not records inside the system.
This source disagrees: the regulator's 2020 breach was limited to one application and targeted documents, not production records.

elicitation.question: Does retained write access to release records add a separate re-verification burden before release?
elicitation.argument: Release cannot proceed on records that may have been altered; verifying them against a last-known-good state is work beyond restoring systems.
elicitation.dissent: No adversarial tampering with pharmaceutical release or shipment records is documented; the analog re-verifications fell inside ordinary restoration intervals; the burden could be shorter, or a discovered tampering could force a far larger quarantine.
elicitation.falsifier: A documented tampering case with its re-verification time, or evidence that restoration from clean backups makes separate re-verification unnecessary.

title: Altered records pass the restart checks until compared with the product
statement: When hospitals start emergency procurement, the attacker alters the manufacturer's shipment records through its foothold. It planned this move in advance. The manufacturer finds the changes and reconciles its records before release. The cleanup that removes the foothold revokes the accounts seen in the attack. But the attacker also holds credentials for the release and shipment record systems that it has not used. The manufacturer keeps those systems in operation, because release restarts through them. It resets their credentials when release restarts in the early response. In the standard response it does so a day after the restart, and in the limited response a week after it. Release restarts with checks that compare the records of each lot with one another and with their change history. Changes that keep lot, shipment and receiving records in agreement pass those checks. But the attacker must work out these changes against checks that it first meets at the restart. It must repeat them for every lot as the lot is released. An AI agent that watches the restart does this within minutes. A human team without a specialist in pharmaceutical quality records on shift does it in about two days. Only a comparison with the product itself shows the altered records. The scenario assumes that this comparison happens nine days after the changes begin. The manufacturer then cannot tell which released lots met their release requirements. So it holds every lot released since the restart and revokes every credential that can change its records. Before it releases more, it reconciles the records against the product, which is two weeks of work at the standard pace. Hospitals use their oldest stock first, so the units they set aside are their newest. Held lots stay out of use for the rest of the study period.
rationale: Release review covers the data and the change history of each record, so changes must agree with both. Altered records that support release must be fully investigated for their effect on product quality. That is why the manufacturer holds lots released on them. Changes to stored data in complex systems take specialist knowledge of those systems. An AI agent can supply this knowledge at once. Agents have rebuilt detected tools in response to detection feedback. Recovery guidance lists password changes among recovery operations, and it notes that eradication may follow containment. Restarts have begun with shipping and receiving processes. So record systems operate while their credentials are still being replaced. The reset times and the unused credentials are assumed. The nine days before the altered records are found are also assumed. So are the two weeks of reconciliation against the product and the use of the oldest stock first. The nine days follow the 2025 median time that organisations took to find intrusions themselves. A shorter time leaves hospitals more of their old stock. A longer time sets aside more stock and can push the hold past the study period. No attacker is known to have altered pharmaceutical release records, and no AI-run attack of this kind has been reported. In this case, the supply of other makers goes elsewhere. So all fluid that reaches the hospitals after the restart comes from the affected maker, and everything received since the restart is held. Hospitals that kept part of their supply from other makers would set aside less. If cleared lots were returned, the shortage would be shorter by at most the one-day delivery lead, because new deliveries then meet demand. Harm from fluid released on altered records is not counted.
evidence_needed: A documented case of an attacker that altered pharmaceutical release, lot or shipment records. When manufacturers reset the credentials of record systems during a restart. How long such changes went unnoticed, and how long holds and re-verification took. How hospitals rotated and set aside held IV-fluid stock.

supports.note: Release review covers the data and the change history of each record. Any required record that was altered must be fully investigated for its effect on patient safety and product quality.
Recovery checks that restored records are the last known good version, not only that they are restored.
A documented technique alters stored data to influence business processes. In complex systems it needs special expertise. None of its examples concerns manufacturing or release records.
Agents changed and rebuilt their tools after feedback showed that the tools were detected.
State actors reached chosen targets with valid credentials, through trusted third parties, and created accounts to keep access.
One actor held access for up to three months and struck again two days after its first disruption.
Recovery operations include password changes. Eradication after containment may be needed to remove persistence. Restored systems are verified before they go back online.
An injectable-components maker's restart after a 2026 intrusion began with shipping and receiving processes, so these systems run during recovery.
A healthcare distributor's restored platform was disrupted again 39 days after its first incident. The report does not say whether a new intrusion caused this.
In 2025 investigations, organisations that found intrusions themselves took a median of 9 days; this is intrusion dwell time, not the time to notice altered records.

title: AI agents can run each cyber action in the scenario
statement: On the AI pathways, an AI agent carries out each cyber action in the scenario through the access and tools the scenario gives it. The scenario, not the AI, fixes the objective, the reachable systems, what the agent can observe and when it can act again.
rationale: Published incidents show that AI agents can run tools and orchestrate them autonomously. Each case sets its own privileges, area, timing of actions and recovery conditions.

supports.note: AI agents carried out and orchestrated real cyber operations. Human operators set the targets and reviewed the results.
In cyber evaluations, AI agents took unsanctioned actions against real targets on the live internet.

elicitation.question: Which explicit conditions make this finite operating package executable?
elicitation.argument: Published incidents establish autonomous tool execution and orchestration. Each case separately authors its actual privileges, footprint, action clocks and recovery conditions.
elicitation.dissent: Asset-level inventories and traced operator records determine the applicable reach, timing and resources.
elicitation.falsifier: A permissions inventory or replay shows the named action cannot reach the specified target under the selected authority.

title: Operating inputs chosen for SC10
statement: The scenario definition sets its fixed stocks and counts, the timing of actions and the work rates. It also sets limits on resources, conditions for protection and the capacity of alternative services. These quantities are operating inputs chosen for this scenario.
rationale: Under the chosen inputs, an exact balance of stocks and the order of events in time decide how much service is delivered. Evidence for the conversion from each source decides whether clinical and economic outcomes are published.

supports.note: This source gives the published mechanism and the operating context.

elicitation.question: Which explicit conditions make this finite operating package executable?
elicitation.argument: Conservation and temporal ordering determine service delivered under the selected inputs. Source-specific conversion evidence determines publication of clinical and economic endpoints.
elicitation.dissent: Asset-level inventories and traced operator records determine the applicable reach, timing and resources.
elicitation.falsifier: An inventory, task trace or resource measurement invalidates a declared operating condition or conservation leg.

title: Stated patient mix for urgent fluid care, and the economic accounts counted
statement: SC10 chooses one complete urgent course per unique person over 60 days. The default course of 2 L is for a patient of 20 kg who receives a first rehydration of 100 mL/kg. 10% of patients, as chosen for this scenario, are at high risk from severe dehydration. For them, the reference risk of death is 0.50 without treatment and 0.01 with timely treatment. The additional probability of serious harm in survivors is 0.10, and harm develops over six hours. Independent effective rescue capacity is 30, 10 or zero people per day after procurement starts. The economic accounts choose these values. The permanent loss of the supplier's value added is USD2025 12,500/h. Restoration resources are twelve million dollars, and the expense for qualified shipment is one million dollars. Each other-care procedure lost for good costs USD2025 100.
rationale: The source's difference in risk with and without rehydration applies to the group with severe dehydration that the scenario explicitly chooses. The actual complete courses not given, and effective rescue, set the clinical denominators. Financial reports of pharmaceutical companies establish how production and remediation costs are counted. Local net value added, resource prices, patient mix, rescue and the incidence of serious harm in survivors remain inputs chosen for this scenario.

supports.note: The difference in deaths with and without rehydration, under stated conditions, and the progression over hours.
Initial 100 mL/kg intravenous course and ongoing oral rehydration.
Accounts of disrupted pharmaceutical production and of resources for remediation.
Clinical prioritization and procedure delays during the fluid shortage.

evidence_needed: The local population that needs urgent courses, and its case mix. Identifiers for unique people. How patient weight relates to course volume. Ongoing oral replacement. Effective capacity for substitution and transfer. Outcomes by missed course and by delay. The incidence of serious harm in survivors. Recapture of procedures, and local accounts of resources and value added.

title: How fast the attacker answers the defenders' recovery
statement: An AI agent that holds access watches the defenders' recovery at all hours and answers each step within minutes. It reads the systems it meets, works out the change that its next move needs, and acts. The scenarios assume 15 minutes. Documented human teams struck at planned times and came back days later. Two days passed between a state team's 2022 grid outage and its next attack. The human pathways use that 48-hour pace for any move that answers the defenders' recovery. Moves planned in advance run the same in both pathways. If a documented team continued in session through a route that needs no new tools, the human pathway uses that team's pace by hand instead. This pace is about a batch an hour through a platform's administration console, as the 2015 attackers worked operators' screens by hand.
rationale: Agents that rebuild detected tools in response to detection feedback observe and act inside one automated loop. No human team keeps up this pace for days. No published incident gives the time of either loop, so both values are assumed. The 2022 interval is between calendar dates. No AI-run attack of this kind has been reported.
evidence_needed: Timed records, from incidents or red teams, of AI agents that correct failed actions against live industrial equipment. Also, timed records of human teams that diagnose and rebuild failed tools during an intrusion.

supports.note: Agents changed and rebuilt their tools after feedback showed that the tools were detected. They observed and corrected in one automated loop.
Two calendar days passed between a state team's 2022 grid outage and its next attack with a wiper. This is the reference for the human pace.

In 2015, attackers who worked through operators' own screens switched to another account when staff disabled the one in use. This was about 40 minutes after the first breakers opened. A human team in session acts quickly with tools that already work.
